matchups.analysis: Rob got absolutely demolished by his own lineup decisions while Flamur coasted to victory despite sabotaging himself worse—Rob benched Kyle Monangai for 27.5 points while starting Michael Wilson's 13.0 dud, losing 14.5 points that could've at least made this interesting, but even that doesn't salvage anything when Flamur's walking away with 120.1 final and 100% win probability. Marcus Mariota's 5.3-point implosion (projected 18.5) finished whatever Rob had left, and the genuinely wild part is Flamur benched Keon Coleman's 20.6 points in favor of Emeka Egbuka's 2.3—he basically threw away 18.3 points and still lapped Rob by 28 because CeeDee Lamb went absolutely nuclear with 32.8 on a 13.7 projection. Both managers made brutal bench decisions, but when your best guy balloons 19 points over projection while the other team's best guy gets 5 on 18.5, the rankings don't matter—Flamur wins this with his eyes closed and takes Rob's dignity with him. ESPN had this locked down from the jump with Flamur at 100% and Rob at a dead 0%, which is about as close to mercy rule as fantasy football gets.

Arben's walking out with this one at 104.0 to 99.9 with 100% win probability—it's done, locked in, no drama left to play. Rinor benched Romeo Doubs' 20.8-point game to start DJ Moore's 2.2-point absolute tire fire, which is the kind of lineup decision that costs you 18.6 points and basically guarantees you're watching the consolation bracket from the couch. Arben didn't exactly nail it either—Courtland Sutton's 0.9 disaster over Jerry Jeudy's 5.1 cost him 4.2 points and makes him look like an idiot—but when your opponent straight-up sabotages himself that hard, you can afford to be a moron and still walk to victory. Chuba Hubbard going off for 25.4 on a 15.1 projection was the only thing keeping Arben from completely imploding, and even that margin of error wasn't enough to save Rinor from the catastrophic bench call that ended this matchup before the games even mattered.

Nori's locked this in at 100% with 121.5 final and all starters done—Adam's staring at 0% and a 12.7-point deficit with nothing left to play, which means this one's already written. The real damage came from Adam benching Tucker Kraft (13.5 pts) to start George Holani (2.5 pts on a 9.2 projection), an 11-point swing that would've at least made this competitive instead of a complete bloodbath. Javonte Williams absolutely carried Nori's week at 28.8 (projected 13.2), but Adam can't even point to bad luck when he actively chose to start a guy who disappeared completely and left his best tight end on the bench—that's the kind of self-sabotage that sticks with you.

Ben's walking away with this at 100% with a locked-in 83.6 final, while Rilind's stuck at 77.7 watching the scoreboard from the bench—that six-point gap is the whole ballgame and it's already decided. Ben actually managed to gift himself this win despite actively trying to sabotage it: benching Malachi Fields (12.2 pts) for Ladd McConkey's beautiful zero on a 9.2 projection means Ben basically won this thing despite his own incompetence, and that's the kind of careless lineup management that usually costs you playoff spots. Rilind didn't help his own cause by benching Brian Thomas Jr. (8.7 pts) to start Dalton Schultz (1.9), but when you're already watching Matthew Stafford collapse from 16.5 projected down to 9.7, that extra six points barely moves the needle on a matchup that was Ben's to lose from the jump—and he almost managed to do it anyway.

Veton got absolutely buried at 1% and deserves every bit of it—benching Rashid Shaheed (11.8) to watch Ja'Marr Chase put up 4.2 points on a 16.5 projection is the kind of lineup decision that should come with a warning label for future drafts. Nico Collins went nuclear for 27.3 (projected 12.6) and that's literally the only thing keeping this from being a complete embarrassment, but when you're down 41.8 points with Brian Robinson Jr. as your last lifeline, you've already lost this matchup twice—once to ESPN's algorithm and once to your own brain. Jetmir and Peter's McMillan explosion (38.2 on 13.5) was the cherry on top of a blowout that was decided the moment you decided Chase was your guy over Shaheed, and no amount of garbage-time rushing yards is closing that gap.

Faton's getting absolutely buried at 15% with a projected 25-point final deficit—that's not a matchup, that's a reckoning. The benching of Rome Odunze (12.4) for Parker Washington's 1.5-point abortion cost him 10.9 points and basically decided this thing before kickoff; even with Drake London and Tyler Shough still cooking, you're asking them to single-handedly outscore Ilir's entire remaining trio of Bijan, Olave, and Juwan Johnson, which isn't happening. Ilir's locking in a comfortable W despite his own bench mistakes (Montgomery at 4.3 instead of Gainwell's 9.7) because his roster is just deeper and better constructed—Carnell Tate going off for 17.0 on a 9.7 projection basically buried the coffin while Faton was busy playing 4D chess with his own lineup and losing.
